extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, practitioners, judges, and law students interested in judicial review under the APA
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of State Farm’s 'hard look' arbitrary-and-capricious standard and how Department of Commerce and Regents clarify requirements for reasoned decision‑making, consideration of alternatives, political influence, and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned decision‑making requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must provide a reasoned explanation for its action; arbitrary and capricious review asks whether the agency 'complied with the procedural requirement that it provide a reasoned explanation for its action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court’s inquiry is to address only whether the agency provided a reasoned explanation, not whether the agency’s decision was wise. (Cited: Regents, Chief Justice Roberts noting review 'unconcerned with the wisdom' of policy.) Agencies must supply a reasoned analysis to justify decisions (State Farm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary and capricious standard under §706(2)(A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review under §706(2)(A) examines whether agency action is arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied via State Farm's hard look review; courts evaluate the adequacy of the agency’s reasoning, consideration of relevant factors, and whether the action is supported by the administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on pretext / implausible rationales
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s explanation may not be 'contrived' or 'incongruent with what the record reveals'; courts may set aside actions grounded in pretext.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department of Commerce set aside the citizenship‑question decision because the sole proffered reason 'seemed contrived' and the record failed to show consideration of that reason. The 'new principle' post‑Commerce: review rejects 'wholly implausible rationale[s]' unsupported by the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternatives / the 'logical response'
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider obvious regulatory alternatives that are 'within the ambit of the existing [policy]' — the 'logical response'—and explain why they are not adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Farm faulted NHTSA for failing to address the obvious airbags‑only alternative when rescinding a passive‑restraint rule. Failure to consider such alternatives can render a decision arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of unstated reasons and political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: A court 'may not reject an agency’s stated reasons for acting simply because the agency might also have had other unstated reasons,' but unstated reasons that render the stated explanation implausible can be problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debated doctrine: some argue courts should credit disclosed political influences (Kagan, Watts); others argue politics are irrelevant so long as stated justifications fall within statutory bounds (Seidenfeld). Department of Commerce emphasized that agencies may have both stated and unstated reasons, but explanations must not be pretextual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support in the administrative record / reliance on relevant data and statutory factors
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s explanations must be supported by relevant available data and by consideration of the factors Congress authorized the agency to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Farm looked for whether NHTSA established, based on 'relevant available motor vehicle safety data,' that the rescission met statutory standards. The Court will scrutinize whether the administrative record supports the proffered rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to consider reliance interests
rubrics_metrics.description: When rescinding a policy, agencies must consider and adequately explain the reliance interests of those affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Justice Roberts found DHS’s rescission of DACA procedurally defective in part because the secretary failed to consider and adequately explain reliance interests weighed against competing policy concerns (Regents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi‑procedural nature of State Farm (procedural with substantive bite)
rubrics_metrics.description: State Farm’s hard look review imposes procedural demands (reasoned explanation) but also may carry substantive requirements about what must appear in the administrative record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garland describes the standard as 'quasi‑procedural' because it requires substantive content in the agency's record though the agency controls how to produce it. This account explains why remand may or may not cure the defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural defect vs substantive defect — remedial consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court identifies a procedural defect (failure to explain/consider), the agency may remedy it on remand; if the defect is substantive (failure to adopt a required policy), the court may foreclose readoption and require a different policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garland’s framework: procedural failures can be fixed by better explanation on remand, permitting the same outcome; substantive failures prevent the agency from reissuing the same policy unless it changes the substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference boundary — courts must not substitute their judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not substitute their own policy judgments for those of agencies; review is not to ask whether the decision was 'the best one possible' or 'better than the alternatives.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted principle from Roberts (and State Farm): judicial role is limited to ensuring reasoned decision‑making, not reweighing policy choices. This principle limits courts from overturning decisions solely because they prefer a different policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible role of politics and disclosure for judicial credit
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate over whether and when political (presidential) influence is an adequate basis for agency action; some argue that disclosure of presidential policy involvement should earn judicial credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kagan and Watts argue that explicit disclosure of presidential involvement can relax scrutiny; Seidenfeld and others argue politics are permissible if the stated justification is within statutory bounds. The page records this unresolved tension and competing scholarly views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruence between stated reasons and record
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s stated reasons must be congruent with the administrative record; an explanation 'incongruent with what the record reveals' supports invalidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department of Commerce invalidated the citizenship question because the secretary’s explanation was inconsistent with what the record showed (Roberts). This is used as a test for pretext and implausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard‑look review as legitimizing mechanism for significant policy changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoned decision‑making and hard look review are intended to protect the public from unreasonable, irrational, poorly justified, and narrowly considered policy changes because agency decisions can have profound consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that because administrative actions (e.g., census question or DACA rescission) have large public impact, courts must apply hard look review to ensure legitimacy, even while the doctrine’s contours remain contested.
